261	# Guion 012: In This World, You Inherit Your Parents' Fears
262	
263	Guion original. Sale de la premisa 17 del banco (`docs/05-guiones-y-fuentes.md`):
264	al cumplir trece recibes el mayor miedo de tu papá. Antes de producirlo, repite
265	la búsqueda del título en YouTube y reescribe a tu gusto el gancho y el remate
266	(hay alternativas al final).
267	
268	- **Tema**: familia (papá e hijo)
269	- **Final**: cómico, con un momento tierno antes del remate
270	- **Regla**: a la medianoche de tu cumpleaños número trece heredas el mayor
271	  miedo de tu papá, y él lo pierde
272	- **Costo de la regla**: el miedo heredado no se puede devolver
273	- **Detalle sembrado**: el mensaje "Home?" que el papá manda todos los días a
274	  las 3:15 y al que el narrador siempre responde "yep" (bloque 3). Se cosecha en
275	  el bloque 7 (no era una manía: era el miedo, y ese "yep" era la mejor parte
276	  del día del papá) y en el remate (ahora los dos se lo mandan)
277	- **Giro**: el mayor miedo del papá bombero nunca fue el fuego, sino que le
278	  pasara algo a la persona que más quiere. Heredado por el hijo, el miedo apunta
279	  al papá. Y al papá le volvió a crecer al minuto: revisó el cuarto del hijo a
280	  las 12:01
281	- **Conteo real**: 367 palabras (18, 59, 49, 51, 78, 26, 50, 36), contadas con script
282	- **Título alterno**: The 3:15 Text
283	
284	Nota de tono: el oficio de bombero se muestra sin incendios en pantalla. La
285	única emergencia que se ve es un gato en un árbol. El granero es "smoky", con
286	humo y sin llamas.
287	
288	## Narración
289	
290	El texto de la narración va en inglés, a ras de margen, listo para pegar en el
291	generador de voz. También está en `012-you-inherit-your-parents-fears.txt`.
292	
293	**[1. Gancho]**
294	
295	In this world, on your thirteenth birthday, you inherit your dad's biggest FEAR, and he loses it FOREVER.
296	
297	**[2. Ejemplos del mundo]**
298	
299	It hits at midnight like a cold hiccup. My friend Odette got her dad's fear of moths. Now he keeps forty of them in the garage. He named them all. Mr. Park passed down his fear of heights and bought a hot air balloon by breakfast. His son can't use the top bunk. And you can't give it BACK.
300	
301	**[3. El ángulo del narrador]**
302	
303	I wasn't worried. My dad is a firefighter. He once carried a full-grown pony out of a smoky barn. He catches wasps with his bare hand. The only weird thing about Dad is a text. Every day at 3:15, he sends me one word. "HOME?" I always answer "yep."
304	
305	**[4. Crisis]**
306	
307	Midnight. Cold hiccup. I felt nothing. Then Dad grabbed his helmet for the night shift, and my knees turned to PUDDING. His biggest fear was never FIRE. It was something happening to the person he loves most. Now it was mine. And the person I love most rides a fire truck.
308	
309	**[5. Tres intentos fallidos]**
310	
311	So I tried to keep him safe. I texted him "home?" forty-six times in one shift. He wrote back, "At work, bud." Not helpful. I hid his car keys in the freezer. He jogged to the station. Four miles. Then I chased the fire truck on my bike, wearing a snorkel. The emergency was a cat in a tree. I climbed up to help. I got stuck. Dad had to rescue me. The cat walked down by itself.
312	
313	**[6. Cuarto intento]**
314	
315	Halfway down the ladder, over his shoulder, I said it. "I'm SCARED all the time now. Every siren. How did you do this for thirteen years?"
316	
317	**[7. Desenlace]**
318	
319	"BADLY," Dad said. "I texted you every day at 3:15." He set me on the grass. "You'd say 'yep.' Best part of my day." So now he was free, right? He laughed. "It was supposed to leave at midnight. I checked your room at 12:01. I think it GREW back."
320	
321	**[8. Remate]**
322	
323	So now we both have it. At 3:15, I text him "home?" He texts me "home?" We both say "yep." Odette got moths. Honestly? Lucky. Someday my kid gets this one. Sorry, kid. Answer your texts.

393	# Guion 013: In This World, Hugs Are Counted
394	
395	Guion original. Sale de la premisa 18 del banco (`docs/05-guiones-y-fuentes.md`):
396	naces con un número fijo de abrazos, y la abuela guardó los suyos. Antes de
397	producirlo, repite la búsqueda del título en YouTube y reescribe a tu gusto el
398	gancho y el remate (hay alternativas al final).
399	
400	- **Tema**: familia (abuela y nieto)
401	- **Final**: emotivo con remate cómico
402	- **Regla**: cada persona nace con mil abrazos exactos y un contador en la
403	  muñeca que baja con cada uno
404	- **Costo de la regla**: cuando llegas a cero no hay más; y solo paga quien abre
405	  los brazos primero (si los dos los abren al tiempo, pagan los dos). El costo
406	  se dice en la segunda frase del bloque 2 y se muestra con la reunión familiar
407	- **Detalle sembrado**: los once abrazos gastados en un muñeco de nieve llamado
408	  Gerald y la abuela que nunca abre los brazos (bloque 3). Se cosecha en el
409	  bloque 7 (la abuela no era fría: ahorraba, y supo para quién al verlo abrazar
410	  al muñeco once veces) y en el remate
411	- **Giro**: el narrador decide gastar su último abrazo en la abuela; ella lo
412	  detiene y abre los brazos primero, así que paga ella. En 81 años nunca fue
413	  la primera: los estaba guardando sin saber para quién
414	- **Conteo real**: 380 palabras (17, 65, 61, 33, 50, 40, 83, 31), contadas con script
415	- **Título alterno**: The Last Hug
416	
417	Nota de tono: la pérdida solo se sugiere ("Her number drops every day", "Neither of
418	us looks at it"). No se muestra enfermedad ni despedida. La abuela termina la
419	historia viva, abrazando.

421	## Narración
422	
423	El texto de la narración va en inglés, a ras de margen, listo para pegar en el
424	generador de voz. También está en `013-hugs-are-counted.txt`.
425	
426	**[1. Gancho]**
427	
428	In this world, you're born with exactly one THOUSAND hugs, and there's a counter on your wrist.
429	
430	**[2. Ejemplos del mundo]**
431	
432	Every hug, it ticks down. But only for whoever opens their arms FIRST. So nobody goes first. My teacher only gives thumbs-ups. At our family reunion, forty people stood around with their arms down for six hours. My uncle cracked at his own wedding. He hit ZERO before the cake. Now he does finger guns. Dogs don't have counters. Nobody knows why. Everybody knows why.
433	
434	**[3. El ángulo del narrador]**
435	
436	I'm a spender. I always go first. When I was five, I used eleven hugs on one snowman. His name was Gerald. I'm fourteen now, and I have FOUR left. My grandma has nine hundred thirty-one. She has never opened her arms. Not once. She just pats your head twice, like she's checking a melon. I figured she didn't like hugs.
437	
438	**[4. Crisis]**
439	
440	Four hugs. For the rest of my life. And Grandma turns eighty-one on Sunday. I wanted to give her one. I also wanted to keep it. So I tried to cheat the counter.
441	
442	**[5. Tres intentos fallidos]**
443	
444	I hugged my mom wearing oven mitts. It counted. THREE. I hugged a tree and waited for it to go first. Trees never go first. TWO. Then my friend Hollis and I counted down and opened at the exact same time. It charged us both. ONE. Hollis is still mad.
445	
446	**[6. Cuarto intento]**
447	
448	On Sunday, I had one hug and one grandma. She sat in her chair with her hands folded. Same as always. I looked at my wrist. Then I decided she was worth it. I walked up and opened my arms.
449	
450	**[7. Desenlace]**
451	
452	She grabbed my wrists. "Put those away," she said. Then she opened hers. WIDE. I'd never seen her do that. Her counter ticked. Nine hundred thirty. Mine still said one. She smelled like peppermint. "Eighty-one years," she said. "I never went first. I was SAVING them. I just didn't know who for. Then I watched a five-year-old hug a snowman eleven times." She's hugged me every morning since. She always goes FIRST. Her number drops every day. Neither of us looks at it.
453	
454	**[8. Remate]**
455	
456	I still have my one. I'm saving it for something huge. Or for Gerald, if it snows. Grandma says that's the dumbest plan she's ever heard. She's knitting him a scarf.

41

161	
162	In this school, rumors paint themselves on the walls, and only come off when somebody says the truth out loud.
163	
164	**[2. Ejemplos del mundo]**
165	
166	The sixth-grade hall once said MR. PELLMAN WEARS A WIG, in green letters two feet tall. He walked up and said, "Yes. His name is Stanley." Gone in one second. The cafeteria wall says THE NUGGETS ARE MOSTLY CARROTS. The lunch lady refuses to comment. It's been up four years.
167	
168	**[3. El ángulo del narrador]**
169	
170	I've never been on a wall. Not one letter. Nine years in this school, and nobody has ever said a word about me. I told myself that was a good thing.
171	
172	**[4. Crisis]**
173	
174	Then Soren showed up. New kid. He could juggle oranges. By Friday, everybody knew his name. So at lunch I said, "I heard he got kicked out of his old school." I made it up. Monday morning, it was on the gym wall. Red letters, six feet tall. Soren stood under it, scrubbing with his sleeve.
175	
176	**[5. Tres intentos fallidos]**
177	
178	I tried to fix it quietly. Tuesday, I used two buckets of soap. The letters just got shinier. Wednesday, I taped a bake sale poster over it. The letters crawled onto the poster. BAKE SALE: SOREN GOT KICKED OUT. Thursday at six a.m., I stood alone in the gym and whispered, "It isn't true." One letter faded. Then it all came back, bigger, and spread across the ceiling. The wall doesn't take half a truth.
179	
180	**[6. Cuarto intento]**
181	
182	Friday, the gym was full. Pep rally. Four hundred kids. I took the microphone from the mascot. "I made it up," I said. My voice shook. "Soren's been here one week and everybody likes him. I've been here nine years, and nobody even knows my middle name."
183	
184	**[7. Desenlace]**
185	
186	The letters peeled off like old tape. The wall went white. Nobody clapped. Soren looked at me for a long time. Then he walked out. Monday, there was new writing over my locker. Small. Blue. HENRIK'S MIDDLE NAME IS PROBABLY SOMETHING COOL. LIKE WOLFGANG. Soren walked past, juggling one orange. He didn't look at me. He was smiling.
187	
188	**[8. Remate]**
189	
190	It's Eugene. I am never saying that out loud. It's the only rumor in this school nobody wants to erase.

The tuba filled up. Third, I got six hundred kids in the gym chanting WE LOVE TOBIN. Lightning hit the flagpole. Twice. Tobin ran.

306	
307	I found him under a library table. I opened my mouth. And for the first time in my life, I CLOSED it. I sat down next to him. I said NOTHING. Not that afternoon. Not all of Thursday. The nurse took my temperature. Tobin said "here" at attendance. I didn't. By noon, the rain stopped. The sky was mine now.

309	**[7. Desenlace]**
310	
311	It wasn't sunny. It was fog. Thick, nervous fog, with one tiny cloud going in circles. Six hundred kids turned around and stared at me. Now they knew what the loud kid looks like on the inside. Tobin looked up at my fog. Then he said three words. "Oh. You TOO?" And he started talking. About frogs. For nineteen minutes. Nobody was watching him. The fog burned off.
312	
313	**[8. Remate]**
314	
315	Friday, I kept my mouth shut. Seventy-four and sunny. Tobin won the sack race, screaming the whole way. We take turns now. I've got the sky on Mondays. Bring a jacket.

392	# Guion 017: In This World, Your Backpack Weighs Your Worries
393	
394	Guion original. Sale de la premisa 28 del banco
395	(`docs/05-guiones-y-fuentes.md`): el morral pesa lo que pesan tus
396	preocupaciones, y el más alegre del salón no puede levantar el suyo.
397	
398	- **Tema**: familia (hermanos) con marco de colegio
399	- **Final**: emotivo, con el peso repartido
400	- **Regla**: tu morral pesa exactamente lo que pesan tus preocupaciones
401	- **Costo de la regla**: vaciarlo no sirve; el peso no está en las cosas y no
402	  desaparece, solo puede pasar al morral de otro
403	- **Detalle sembrado**: "el mío flota; me lo amarro a la muñeca y mi papá me
404	  dice la cometa" (bloque 3). Se cosecha en el desenlace (flotaba porque su
405	  hermano menor cargaba su mitad) y en el remate (ya nadie le dice la cometa).
406	  La linterna de rana (bloque 5) se cosecha en el desenlace.
407	- **Giro**: el niño más alegre de cuarto carga las preocupaciones que le
408	  tocaban a su hermano mayor; el narrador no le quita el peso con chistes sino
409	  recibiéndolo en su propio morral
410	- **Conteo real**: 357 palabras (17, 44, 53, 38, 52, 59, 64, 30), contadas con script
411	- **Título alterno**: The Kite
412

414	
415	El texto de la narración va en inglés, a ras de margen, listo para pegar en el
416	generador de voz. También está en `017-backpack-weighs-your-worries.txt`.
417	
418	**[1. Gancho]**
419	
420	In this world, your backpack weighs exactly as much as your WORRIES, and emptying it doesn't HELP.
421	
422	**[2. Ejemplos del mundo]**
423	
424	My math teacher wheels hers in on a cart. During finals week, the school bus drags sparks down the road. Babies' diaper bags float. Parents tie them to the stroller like balloons. My grandma's purse weighs nothing. She says she ran out at seventy.
425	
426	**[3. El ángulo del narrador]**
427	
428	Mine FLOATS too. I'm fifteen, and I tie my backpack to my wrist so it won't blow away. Dad calls me "the kite." My little brother Benji is the happiest kid in fourth grade. Gap-tooth grin. Sings to the toaster. And every morning, he drags his bag to the bus with both hands.
429	
430	**[4. Crisis]**
431	
432	The morning he left for Camp Wobbly Pine, his bag wouldn't MOVE at all. It had cracked his bedroom floor. The bus left at eight. It was 7:31. Benji kept grinning. "It's FINE! I'll just live here now."
433	
434	**[5. Tres intentos fallidos]**
435	
436	I told him my best joke. He laughed for a full minute. The bag lost four ounces. So I emptied it. Two socks, a toothbrush, a frog flashlight. Still stuck. So I tied it to Dad's riding mower and hit the gas. The mower did a wheelie. The bag didn't budge. 7:48.
437	
438	**[6. Cuarto intento]**
439	
440	So I sat on the floor next to it. "Benji. What's in there?" He stopped grinning. "You wouldn't get it. Yours FLOATS." I untied my bag from my wrist and unzipped it. "Then put ONE in mine." He looked at me for a while. "Mom's car makes a noise." My bag dropped an inch. "Okay. That one's MINE now."
441	
442	**[7. Desenlace]**
443	
444	He kept going. Dad's job. The stove. If I'd pass math. If I packed my lunch. If I'd forget him when I got my license. Six worries. Half of them were about me. My bag hit the floor so hard the frog flashlight turned on. Benji picked his up with one hand. Mine had been floating for years because he was carrying my HALF.
445	
446	**[8. Remate]**
447	
448	He made the bus by nine seconds. My backpack weighs nineteen pounds now. I checked the stove twice today. Dad stopped calling me the kite. BEST backache I've ever had.

# Guion 014: In This School, Your Grades Appear on Your Forehead

Guion original. Sale de la premisa 22 del banco
(`docs/05-guiones-y-fuentes.md`): todos ven tu nota en la frente, y la más
inteligente del colegio tiene un signo de pregunta.

- **Tema**: colegio (miedo a equivocarse)
- **Final**: cómico y tierno
- **Regla**: tu nota brilla en tu frente y nada la tapa
- **Costo de la regla**: no se puede esconder, y la frente solo califica lo que
  entregas; lo que nunca entregas te deja en signo de pregunta
- **Detalle sembrado**: el borrador del tamaño de un sándwich y el signo de
  pregunta "desde tercero" (bloque 3). Se cosechan en el bloque 6 (412 exámenes
  perfectos que nunca entregó) y en el remate (el borrador termina de tope de
  puerta). También se cosecha la cuchara de Devon (bloque 2) en el remate.
- **Giro**: la más inteligente no tiene nota porque le aterra que una letra la
  defina; el narrador, un C orgulloso, se deja bajar a D delante de todos para
  mostrarle que se sobrevive
- **Conteo real**: 388 palabras (18, 48, 46, 33, 77, 85, 49, 32), contadas con script
- **Título alterno**: The Question Mark

## Narración

El texto de la narración va en inglés, a ras de margen, listo para pegar en el
generador de voz. También está en `014-grades-on-your-forehead.txt`.

**[1. Gancho]**

In this school, your grade glows on your FOREHEAD, and no hat in the world can cover it.

**[2. Ejemplos del mundo]**

Hats, bangs, a ski mask. It shines right through. Devon got one A-plus and walked into a locker, staring at himself in a spoon. Our principal still has a faded B-minus up there. He tells people it's a birthmark. Mine is a C. A big, orange, friendly C.

**[3. El ángulo del narrador]**

Then there's Winnie Okafor. Smartest kid in the building. She corrects the textbook in pen. But her forehead doesn't show a letter. It shows a QUESTION MARK. It has since third grade. She also carries an eraser the size of a sandwich. I never wondered why.

**[4. Crisis]**

Then Mr. Haskell made us science fair partners. Partners share ONE grade. Due Friday. One D, and I'd repeat his class, including the forty-minute slideshow about gravel. I wasn't worried. I had Winnie.

**[5. Tres intentos fallidos]**

Monday, she built a volcano. Real smoke. I yelled, "Done! Hand it in!" She tore it down. The lava was "the WRONG orange." Wednesday, she built the solar system. Eight planets, spinning. I told her it was perfect. WRONG word. She found Neptune two millimeters off. Thursday, she built a robot that folds socks. I grabbed it and ran for Mr. Haskell's room. I made it nine steps. The robot folded my sock. I was wearing it.

**[6. Cuarto intento]**

She shoved the robot in her locker. That's when I saw inside. Tests. Four hundred and twelve of them. All perfect. NONE turned in. "If I never hand it in," she whispered, "it can't be WRONG." So Friday, I went first. A potato, two wires, and a light bulb. The bulb did not light. My C flickered and dropped to a D. In front of everybody. I pointed at my forehead and looked right at Winnie. "See? STILL HERE. I even had a sandwich today."

**[7. Desenlace]**

Her hands shook. She pulled one page from her bag and set it on the desk. Her question mark spun like a loading wheel. Then it stopped. B-PLUS. She forgot to write her name. The whole class gasped. Winnie touched her forehead. Then she laughed so hard she snorted.

**[8. Remate]**

Averaged with my potato, we both got a C. Winnie checks hers in every spoon she passes. Her giant eraser is my doorstop now. And she has never once tried a hat.

#### FILE 015-rumors-become-graffiti.md
# Guion 015: In This School, Rumors Become Graffiti

Guion original. Sale de la premisa 23 del banco
(`docs/05-guiones-y-fuentes.md`): cada chisme se escribe solo en las paredes y
solo se borra diciendo la verdad en voz alta.

- **Tema**: colegio (un chisme inventado y la envidia de quien nadie nombra)
- **Final**: redención con ironía (el narrador recibe su primer chisme y decide
  no borrarlo)
- **Regla**: todo chisme se pinta solo en las paredes del colegio
- **Costo de la regla**: solo se borra cuando alguien dice la verdad completa
  en voz alta; ni jabón, ni carteles, ni medias verdades sirven
- **Detalle sembrado**: "nunca he salido en una pared, ni una letra" (bloque
  3). Se cosecha en el desenlace (aparece su primer grafiti) y en el remate (es
  el único chisme que nadie quiere borrar)
- **Giro**: el narrador inventó el chisme por envidia de ser invisible; al
  confesarlo, el niño al que le hizo daño le regala lo único que nunca tuvo:
  que alguien hable de él
- **Conteo real**: 357 palabras (20, 50, 31, 56, 75, 47, 58, 20), contadas con script
- **Título alterno**: The Gym Wall

## Narración

El texto de la narración va en inglés, a ras de margen, listo para pegar en el
generador de voz. También está en `015-rumors-become-graffiti.txt`.

**[1. Gancho]**

In this school, rumors paint themselves on the walls, and only come off when somebody says the truth out loud.

**[2. Ejemplos del mundo]**

The sixth-grade hall once said MR. PELLMAN WEARS A WIG, in green letters two feet tall. He walked up and said, "Yes. His name is Stanley." Gone in one second. The cafeteria wall says THE NUGGETS ARE MOSTLY CARROTS. The lunch lady refuses to comment. It's been up four years.

**[3. El ángulo del narrador]**

I've never been on a wall. Not one letter. Nine years in this school, and nobody has ever said a word about me. I told myself that was a good thing.

**[4. Crisis]**

Then Soren showed up. New kid. He could juggle oranges. By Friday, everybody knew his name. So at lunch I said, "I heard he got kicked out of his old school." I made it up. Monday morning, it was on the gym wall. Red letters, six feet tall. Soren stood under it, scrubbing with his sleeve.

**[5. Tres intentos fallidos]**

I tried to fix it quietly. Tuesday, I used two buckets of soap. The letters just got shinier. Wednesday, I taped a bake sale poster over it. The letters crawled onto the poster. BAKE SALE: SOREN GOT KICKED OUT. Thursday at six a.m., I stood alone in the gym and whispered, "It isn't true." One letter faded. Then it all came back, bigger, and spread across the ceiling. The wall doesn't take half a truth.

**[6. Cuarto intento]**

Friday, the gym was full. Pep rally. Four hundred kids. I took the microphone from the mascot. "I made it up," I said. My voice shook. "Soren's been here one week and everybody likes him. I've been here nine years, and nobody even knows my middle name."

**[7. Desenlace]**

The letters peeled off like old tape. The wall went white. Nobody clapped. Soren looked at me for a long time. Then he walked out. Monday, there was new writing over my locker. Small. Blue. HENRIK'S MIDDLE NAME IS PROBABLY SOMETHING COOL. LIKE WOLFGANG. Soren walked past, juggling one orange. He didn't look at me. He was smiling.

**[8. Remate]**

It's Eugene. I am never saying that out loud. It's the only rumor in this school nobody wants to erase.

#### FILE 016-quietest-kid-controls-the-weather.md
# Guion 016: In This School, the Quietest Kid Controls the Weather

Guion original. Sale de la premisa 25 del banco
(`docs/05-guiones-y-fuentes.md`): el clima del colegio depende del ánimo de
quien menos habla.

- **Tema**: colegio (el niño callado y el niño que no se calla)
- **Final**: cálido y cómico, con intercambio de papeles
- **Regla**: el clima sobre el colegio sigue el ánimo del que menos habla
- **Costo de la regla**: el más callado no puede esconder lo que siente; cada
  vez que se mueve una nube, 600 niños voltean a mirarlo
- **Detalle sembrado**: "yo soy el que más habla, así que el cielo nunca ha
  sido mi problema" y el récord de 19 minutos sin respirar (bloque 3). Se
  cosechan en el bloque 6 (al callarse, el cielo pasa a ser suyo) y en el
  desenlace (Tobin habla 19 minutos)
- **Giro**: el narrador se calla un día entero para quitarle el cielo de
  encima a Tobin, y el colegio entero ve lo que siente por dentro el que más
  habla: niebla nerviosa
- **Conteo real**: 364 palabras (18, 64, 26, 40, 57, 60, 68, 31), contadas con script
- **Título alterno**: The Weather Kid

## Narración

El texto de la narración va en inglés, a ras de margen, listo para pegar en el
generador de voz. También está en `016-quietest-kid-controls-the-weather.txt`.

**[1. Gancho]**

In this school, the weather over the building follows the MOOD of the kid who talks the LEAST.

**[2. Ejemplos del mundo]**

That kid is Tobin. He said eleven words all last year. Nine of them were "here." When he aced a spelling test, we got sun for a week. When he dropped his sandwich, it hailed on the parking lot. Our weather app is just a photo of his face. And every time a cloud moves, six hundred kids turn around and stare at him.

**[3. El ángulo del narrador]**

Me, I talk the MOST. Teachers have timed it. My record is nineteen minutes without a breath. So the sky has never once been my problem.

**[4. Crisis]**

Then came Field Day week. It rained nine days straight. Principal Ruiz said if it rained Friday, Field Day became a three-hour assembly about fire exits. Everybody looked at Tobin. Then everybody looked at me. "I'll fix him," I said.

**[5. Tres intentos fallidos]**

First, cupcakes. Fourteen of them, stacked on his desk. We got four minutes of sun. Then fog. Second, the marching band played his favorite song under his window. Hail, the size of meatballs. The tuba filled up. Third, I got six hundred kids in the gym chanting WE LOVE TOBIN. Lightning hit the flagpole. Twice. Tobin ran.

**[6. Cuarto intento]**

I found him under a library table. I opened my mouth. And for the first time in my life, I CLOSED it. I sat down next to him. I said NOTHING. Not that afternoon. Not all of Thursday. The nurse took my temperature. Tobin said "here" at attendance. I didn't. By noon, the rain stopped. The sky was mine now.

**[7. Desenlace]**

It wasn't sunny. It was fog. Thick, nervous fog, with one tiny cloud going in circles. Six hundred kids turned around and stared at me. Now they knew what the loud kid looks like on the inside. Tobin looked up at my fog. Then he said three words. "Oh. You TOO?" And he started talking. About frogs. For nineteen minutes. Nobody was watching him. The fog burned off.

**[8. Remate]**

Friday, I kept my mouth shut. Seventy-four and sunny. Tobin won the sack race, screaming the whole way. We take turns now. I've got the sky on Mondays. Bring a jacket.

#### FILE 017-backpack-weighs-your-worries.md
# Guion 017: In This World, Your Backpack Weighs Your Worries

Guion original. Sale de la premisa 28 del banco
(`docs/05-guiones-y-fuentes.md`): el morral pesa lo que pesan tus
preocupaciones, y el más alegre del salón no puede levantar el suyo.

- **Tema**: familia (hermanos) con marco de colegio
- **Final**: emotivo, con el peso repartido
- **Regla**: tu morral pesa exactamente lo que pesan tus preocupaciones
- **Costo de la regla**: vaciarlo no sirve; el peso no está en las cosas y no
  desaparece, solo puede pasar al morral de otro
- **Detalle sembrado**: "el mío flota; me lo amarro a la muñeca y mi papá me
  dice la cometa" (bloque 3). Se cosecha en el desenlace (flotaba porque su
  hermano menor cargaba su mitad) y en el remate (ya nadie le dice la cometa).
  La linterna de rana (bloque 5) se cosecha en el desenlace.
- **Giro**: el niño más alegre de cuarto carga las preocupaciones que le
  tocaban a su hermano mayor; el narrador no le quita el peso con chistes sino
  recibiéndolo en su propio morral

## Narración

El texto de la narración va en inglés, a ras de margen, listo para pegar en el
generador de voz. También está en `017-backpack-weighs-your-worries.txt`.

**[1. Gancho]**

In this world, your backpack weighs exactly as much as your WORRIES, and emptying it doesn't HELP.

**[2. Ejemplos del mundo]**

My math teacher wheels hers in on a cart. During finals week, the school bus drags sparks down the road. Babies' diaper bags float. Parents tie them to the stroller like balloons. My grandma's purse weighs nothing. She says she ran out at seventy.

**[3. El ángulo del narrador]**

Mine FLOATS too. I'm fifteen, and I tie my backpack to my wrist so it won't blow away. Dad calls me "the kite." My little brother Benji is the happiest kid in fourth grade. Gap-tooth grin. Sings to the toaster. And every morning, he drags his bag to the bus with both hands.

**[4. Crisis]**

The morning he left for Camp Wobbly Pine, his bag wouldn't MOVE at all. It had cracked his bedroom floor. The bus left at eight. It was 7:31. Benji kept grinning. "It's FINE! I'll just live here now."

**[5. Tres intentos fallidos]**

I told him my best joke. He laughed for a full minute. The bag lost four ounces. So I emptied it. Two socks, a toothbrush, a frog flashlight. Still stuck. So I tied it to Dad's riding mower and hit the gas. The mower did a wheelie. The bag didn't budge. 7:48.

**[6. Cuarto intento]**

So I sat on the floor next to it. "Benji. What's in there?" He stopped grinning. "You wouldn't get it. Yours FLOATS." I untied my bag from my wrist and unzipped it. "Then put ONE in mine." He looked at me for a while. "Mom's car makes a noise." My bag dropped an inch. "Okay. That one's MINE now."

**[7. Desenlace]**

He kept going. Dad's job. The stove. If I'd pass math. If I packed my lunch. If I'd forget him when I got my license. Six worries. Half of them were about me. My bag hit the floor so hard the frog flashlight turned on. Benji picked his up with one hand. Mine had been floating for years because he was carrying my HALF.

**[8. Remate]**

He made the bus by nine seconds. My backpack weighs nineteen pounds now. I checked the stove twice today. Dad stopped calling me the kite. BEST backache I've ever had.

319	In this town, nobody opens the door after the THIRD knock.
320	
321	**[2. Ejemplos del mundo]** (82 palabras)
322	
323	Two knocks is a neighbor. THREE knocks is something else. Nobody knows what, because nobody has opened in sixty-one years. So everybody here knocks twice. The mailman. The pizza guy. A woodpecker got a ticket. The thing that knocks three times picks one house. Always the newest family in town. Then it comes back every night at 9:14. And nobody visits a house that's got it. The Pruitts had it for six years. They finally moved. It knocked on the moving truck.
324	
325	**[3. El ángulo del narrador]** (48 palabras)
326	
327	We moved here in June. My fifth town in six years. New families here always get a welcome pie. We got nothing. Because on our first night, at 9:14, there it was. Knock. Knock. Knock. The third one is always softer than the first two. Like it's SORRY.
328	
329	**[4. Crisis]** (49 palabras)
330	
331	Four months later, my little brother Otis sleeps in the bathtub. It's the farthest spot from the front door. Then Mom started taping up boxes. "We leave Friday," she said. I had just unpacked my last one. I was not going to be the new kid a sixth time.
332	
333	**[5. Tres intentos fallidos]** (76 palabras)
334	
335	So I tried to make it stop. Monday, I taped a sign on the door. NOBODY HOME. It knocked three times on the sign. Tuesday, I slept with two pillows over my head. It knocked on my window. My room is on the second floor. Wednesday, I yelled through the door. "Go away! Nobody wants you here!" Ten seconds of nothing. Then three knocks, so quiet I almost missed them. Somehow that was the worst one.
336	
337	**[6. Cuarto intento]** (60 palabras)
338	
339	Thursday night, I sat on the floor with my back against the door. 9:14. Knock. Knock. Knock. And I said, "I'm sorry I yelled. I've been the new kid five times. I know what it's like to stand outside and hope somebody opens." Nothing. So I did the one thing you never do in this town. I OPENED the door.
340	
341	**[7. Desenlace]** (86 palabras)
342	
343	It was nine feet tall. A long gray raincoat with nothing inside but fog. No face. And it was holding a pie. Its hands shook so hard the tin rattled. There was a card on top. WELCOME TO TOWN, in handwriting from sixty-one years ago. I asked, "Why three knocks?" It looked down at where its feet should be. Its voice sounded like an old hinge. "TWO is for neighbors." It didn't think it was one. I said, "You've lived here longer than anybody. Knock TWICE."
344

346	
347	We unpacked the boxes. Otis sleeps in a bed again. We did not eat the pie. That pie is older than my grandpa. But every night at 9:14, there are two knocks on our door. And somebody always opens.

# Guion 018: The Echo

Guion original de terror suave. Sale de la premisa 29 del banco
(`docs/05-guiones-y-fuentes.md`): en este pueblo el eco no repite lo que
dices, sino lo que de verdad piensas.

- **Tema**: terror suave, familia (una hija y su papá después de perder a la
  mamá)
- **Final**: emotivo, con un último plano de escalofrío dulce
- **Regla**: el eco del pueblo no repite lo que gritas; dice lo que de verdad
  piensas
- **Costo de la regla**: responde con tu propia voz, un respiro después, y
  todo el pueblo lo oye; por eso todos viven susurrando
- **Detalle sembrado**: la mamá era la única a la que el eco le devolvía sus
  palabras exactas, "Goodnight, bug" (bloque 3). Se cosecha en el desenlace
  (el eco repite "We miss you" palabra por palabra) y en el remate (el eco
  dice "Goodnight, bug" sin que nadie grite)
- **Giro**: la voz que asusta al pueblo de madrugada es el papá, que sube
  cada noche a gritar "estoy bien" esperando que el eco por fin le dé la
  razón; la hija lo salva dejando que el eco diga su propio miedo delante de
  él
- **Conteo real**: 440 palabras (16, 80, 54, 40, 107, 58, 45, 40), contadas con script
- **Título alterno**: In This Town, the Echo Says What You Really Think

## Narración

El texto de la narración va en inglés, a ras de margen, listo para pegar en el
generador de voz. También está en `018-the-echo.txt`.

**[1. Gancho]**

In this town, the echo doesn't repeat what you say. It says what you really think.

**[2. Ejemplos del mundo]**

It lives in the Notch, a crack in the hills past the last streetlight. It answers in your own voice, one breath late, and the whole town hears it. Mr. Dabney once yelled, "I love it here!" The Notch said, "I'd leave tomorrow." He moved in June. Our mayor gave one speech up there. That's why we have a new mayor. So we whisper. All of us. We clap at football games like it's golf. Even the dogs bark quietly.

**[3. El ángulo del narrador]**

Only one person ever got her own words back. My mom. Every night she leaned off the back porch and yelled, "Goodnight, bug!" And the hills said it right back, word for word. We lost her last winter. Now Dad says the same thing every morning. "We're doing great, kiddo." Thumbs up. Burnt toast.

**[4. Crisis]**

Then the night echoes started. 2:07 a.m. A man's voice rolled down off the hills, loud enough to rattle the spoons. "I can't do this." Nobody heard a shout. Just the answer. Every dog in town went under a bed.

**[5. Tres intentos fallidos]**

The second night, it came again. "The house is too quiet." Forty windows lit up at once. I got up and checked Dad's room. The bed was empty. His boots were gone. The third night, I followed his boot prints up the trail with a flashlight. The fog swallowed the beam three feet out. Somebody was shouting up ahead. I found him at the edge of the Notch, hands cupped around his mouth. "I'M FINE!" he yelled into the dark. One breath. Then the dark answered in his voice. "I don't know how to be both of them." He yelled it seven times. It never once agreed.

**[6. Cuarto intento]**

I stepped up beside him. He jumped. "Go home, kiddo. We're doing great." Thumbs up. His thumb was shaking. So I turned to the Notch and yelled the only thing I had. "I'M FINE TOO!" One breath. Then my own voice came back, small and clear. "I hear you leave every night. I'm scared you won't come back."

**[7. Desenlace]**

Dad's thumb came down. He didn't say anything. He just took my hand. Then we yelled together, as loud as we could. "WE MISS YOU!" One breath. And the hills did something they hadn't done in a year. They said it back. Word for word.

**[8. Remate]**

The night echoes stopped. Dad still burns the toast, but he quit the thumbs up. And last night, half asleep, I heard the hills one more time. Two words. "Goodnight, bug." Nobody had yelled it. Somebody was just thinking it.

#### FILE 019-the-night-trade.md
# Guion 019: The Night Trade

Guion original de terror suave. Sale de la premisa 31 del banco
(`docs/05-guiones-y-fuentes.md`): algo se lleva un objeto de tu casa cada
noche y deja uno que perdiste hace años.

- **Tema**: terror suave, familia (una nieta y su abuela que empieza a
  olvidar)
- **Final**: agridulce, con un último plano de escalofrío y sonrisa
- **Regla**: cada noche algo se lleva una cosa de tu casa y deja una que
  perdiste hace años
- **Costo de la regla**: el cambio siempre es parejo (pequeño por pequeño,
  grande por grande) y tú no escoges qué se lleva ni qué devuelve
- **Detalle sembrado**: la abuela le deja una taza de té al "visitante de la
  noche"; el té desaparece, la taza nunca (bloque 3). Y el apodo "Pidge", que
  la abuela perdió en marzo (bloque 3). Se cosechan en el desenlace ("Pidge")
  y en el remate (la taza vuelve lavada)
- **Giro**: la narradora deja de ofrecer cosas y ofrece algo suyo sin
  preguntar qué; recibe una sola mañana con su abuela de vuelta, y a cambio
  queda un cuadrado limpio en el polvo de su repisa: no sabe qué le falta,
  igual que su abuela
- **Conteo real**: 471 palabras (20, 83, 55, 36, 102, 85, 48, 42), contadas con script
- **Título alterno**: In This Town, Something Takes One Thing Every Night

## Narración

El texto de la narración va en inglés, a ras de margen, listo para pegar en el
generador de voz. También está en `019-the-night-trade.txt`.

**[1. Gancho]**

In this town, something takes ONE thing from your house every night, and leaves one thing you LOST years ago.

**[2. Ejemplos del mundo]**

It comes at three a.m. You never see it. You just hear a drawer slide open, slow. It took our TV remote and left a sock I lost in second grade. The sock was still wet. It took Dad's car keys and left his retainer from high school. The Fitzgeralds lost a couch and got back a hamster. The hamster looked like it had seen things. The trade is always FAIR. Small for small. Big for big. And you don't get to pick.

**[3. El ángulo del narrador]**

My Nana isn't scared of it. She calls it "our night guest" and leaves a cup of tea by the pantry. By morning, the tea is gone. The cup never is. Nana used to call me Pidge. Since March, she calls me "the NICE GIRL." She lost my name somewhere, and she can't find it.

**[4. Crisis]**

So I had an idea. If our night guest brings back lost things, it could bring back that. Dad says by summer, she might lose his name too. I just had to offer something big enough.

**[5. Tres intentos fallidos]**

Night one, I left my bike by the pantry. In the morning, there was a tricycle I lost when I was four. Still muddy. Nana patted my hand. "Thank you, nice girl." Night two, I left my phone. I got Nana's reading glasses, missing since 2015. She put them on and read me the cereal box. Twice. Night three, I left everything. My savings jar, two hundred and twelve dollars. My trophies. The TV. In the morning, the kitchen was full. Forty-one umbrellas. Nine library books. Every mitten our family ever dropped. Nana clapped. "What a lovely sale. Do you work here?"

**[6. Cuarto intento]**

Night four, I left NOTHING. I sat at the kitchen table in the dark and waited. 2:59. The fridge stopped humming. 3:00. The pantry door opened by itself, one inch. The air went cold. Something was breathing in there, slow, like a drawer sliding. I didn't look. "I don't have anything left," I whispered. "So take something of mine. Anything. I won't even ask what. Just give her back one morning." The breathing stopped. The tea went down, like somebody sipping. The door clicked shut.

**[7. Desenlace]**

In the morning, the table was empty. First time ever. Nana shuffled in, squinting at the floor. "PIDGE," she said. "Why is there a tricycle in my kitchen?" I couldn't talk. She made pancakes. She beat me at cards, cheating. By dinner, I was "the nice girl" again.

**[8. Remate]**

There's a clean square in the dust on my shelf. I don't know what used to sit there. Now I know how Nana feels. It still takes one thing every night. But last night, for the first time, it WASHED the cup.

# Guion 020: In This Town, Nobody Opens After the Third Knock

Guion original. Sale de la premisa 32 del banco (`docs/05-guiones-y-fuentes.md`,
sección de terror suave). Conteo real con script: **451 palabras** (rango
pedido para terror suave: 400 a 480). A 240 palabras por minuto son cerca de
113 segundos.

- **Tema**: terror suave, ser el nuevo del pueblo
- **Final**: emotivo y cálido, con remate tierno
- **Regla**: nadie abre la puerta después del tercer golpe; dos golpes es un
  vecino, tres es "otra cosa"
- **Costo de la regla**: lo que toca tres veces escoge una casa (siempre la de
  la familia más nueva), vuelve cada noche a las 9:14 y nadie visita esa casa
- **Detalle sembrado**: "siempre escoge a la familia más nueva" y "a las
  familias nuevas les llevan un pie de bienvenida; a nosotros, nada" (bloques
  2 y 3), más "el tercer golpe siempre es más suave, como si pidiera perdón".
  Se cosechan en el bloque 7: la criatura lleva 61 años tratando de entregar
  un pie de bienvenida
- **Giro**: toca tres veces porque "dos es para los vecinos" y nunca creyó que
  la dejaran serlo. El monstruo del pueblo era el único que vino a saludar
- **Conteo real**: 451 palabras (11, 82, 48, 49, 76, 60, 86, 39), contadas con script
- **Título alterno**: The Third Knock

## Narración

El texto de la narración va en inglés, a ras de margen, listo para pegar en el
generador de voz. También está en `020-nobody-opens-after-the-third-knock.txt`.

**[1. Gancho]** (11 palabras)

In this town, nobody opens the door after the THIRD knock.

**[2. Ejemplos del mundo]** (82 palabras)

Two knocks is a neighbor. THREE knocks is something else. Nobody knows what, because nobody has opened in sixty-one years. So everybody here knocks twice. The mailman. The pizza guy. A woodpecker got a ticket. The thing that knocks three times picks one house. Always the newest family in town. Then it comes back every night at 9:14. And nobody visits a house that's got it. The Pruitts had it for six years. They finally moved. It knocked on the moving truck.

**[3. El ángulo del narrador]** (48 palabras)

We moved here in June. My fifth town in six years. New families here always get a welcome pie. We got nothing. Because on our first night, at 9:14, there it was. Knock. Knock. Knock. The third one is always softer than the first two. Like it's SORRY.

**[4. Crisis]** (49 palabras)

Four months later, my little brother Otis sleeps in the bathtub. It's the farthest spot from the front door. Then Mom started taping up boxes. "We leave Friday," she said. I had just unpacked my last one. I was not going to be the new kid a sixth time.

**[5. Tres intentos fallidos]** (76 palabras)

So I tried to make it stop. Monday, I taped a sign on the door. NOBODY HOME. It knocked three times on the sign. Tuesday, I slept with two pillows over my head. It knocked on my window. My room is on the second floor. Wednesday, I yelled through the door. "Go away! Nobody wants you here!" Ten seconds of nothing. Then three knocks, so quiet I almost missed them. Somehow that was the worst one.

**[6. Cuarto intento]** (60 palabras)

Thursday night, I sat on the floor with my back against the door. 9:14. Knock. Knock. Knock. And I said, "I'm sorry I yelled. I've been the new kid five times. I know what it's like to stand outside and hope somebody opens." Nothing. So I did the one thing you never do in this town. I OPENED the door.

**[7. Desenlace]** (86 palabras)

It was nine feet tall. A long gray raincoat with nothing inside but fog. No face. And it was holding a pie. Its hands shook so hard the tin rattled. There was a card on top. WELCOME TO TOWN, in handwriting from sixty-one years ago. I asked, "Why three knocks?" It looked down at where its feet should be. Its voice sounded like an old hinge. "TWO is for neighbors." It didn't think it was one. I said, "You've lived here longer than anybody. Knock TWICE."

**[8. Remate]** (39 palabras)

We unpacked the boxes. Otis sleeps in a bed again. We did not eat the pie. That pie is older than my grandpa. But every night at 9:14, there are two knocks on our door. And somebody always opens.

#### FILE 021-forgotten-things-go-to-the-basement.md
# Guion 021: In This World, Forgotten Things Go to the Basement

Guion original. Sale de la premisa 34 del banco (`docs/05-guiones-y-fuentes.md`,
sección de terror suave). Conteo real con script: **479 palabras** (rango
pedido: 400 a 480). A 240 palabras por minuto son cerca de 120 segundos.

- **Tema**: terror suave, familia (nieto y abuela)
- **Final**: emotivo (nudo en la garganta) con remate tierno y cómico
- **Regla**: todo lo que olvidas aparece en tu sótano, en una repisa y con una
  etiqueta de papel
- **Costo de la regla**: nadie puede subir lo que otro olvidó; solo sube
  cuando su dueño lo recuerda por su cuenta
- **Detalle sembrado**: la abuela todavía le corta los bordes al sándwich y le
  dice Dino por la capa verde de dinosaurio que usó a los siete años (bloque
  3). Se cosecha en los bloques 6 y 7 y en el remate
- **Giro**: la abuela no olvidó a su nieto; olvidó que creció. Por eso el que
  está en el sótano es el narrador de quince años, no el niño
- **Conteo real**: 479 palabras (11, 74, 62, 71, 81, 89, 52, 39), contadas con script
- **Título alterno**: The Bottom Step

## Narración

El texto de la narración va en inglés, a ras de margen, listo para pegar en el
generador de voz. También está en `021-forgotten-things-go-to-the-basement.txt`.

**[1. Gancho]** (11 palabras)

In this world, everything you forget ends up in your basement.

**[2. Ejemplos del mundo]** (74 palabras)

Keys. Homework. The name of that one actor. You go downstairs and there it is, on a shelf with a paper tag. My dad's basement has four hundred passwords and one wedding anniversary. Mom knew exactly which shelf. Our dog forgot a tennis ball in 2019. He still visits it. But there's a catch. You can't carry somebody else's forgotten thing back upstairs. It only comes up when they remember it on their own.

**[3. El ángulo del narrador]** (62 palabras)

My grandma lives two streets over. She calls me Dino. When I was seven, I wore a green dinosaur cape for a whole year. I'm fifteen now, and she still cuts the crusts off my sandwiches. I've wanted to tell her to stop since sixth grade. Lately her basement has been filling up. Her glasses. Her lemon cake recipe. The word "umbrella."

**[4. Crisis]** (71 palabras)

Last Sunday she smiled at me like I was the mailman. "Can I help you, young man?" I laughed. She didn't. So I went down to her basement. Fourteen steps. It was colder than it should have been. Somebody was sitting on the bottom step, facing the wall. Gray hoodie. My hoodie. It turned around. It was me. Same scab on my chin. And a paper tag on its wrist. ARLO.

**[5. Tres intentos fallidos]** (81 palabras)

So I tried to bring me back up. I showed her forty photos of us. She said, "What a handsome boy. His grandma must be proud." Then I taped my school ID to her fridge. By lunch it was on a basement shelf. Then I took the other me by the hand and pulled him upstairs. Step eleven. Step twelve. On step thirteen he went thin, like breath on a window. Then he was back at the bottom, facing the wall.

**[6. Cuarto intento]** (89 palabras)

I sat down at her kitchen table. She put a plate in front of me. A sandwich, crusts cut off. "My grandson likes them like this," she said. "He's about this tall." Her hand stopped at the edge of the counter. She hadn't forgotten me. She forgot I grew up. So I quit trying to make her remember fifteen. I dug the green cape out of her hall closet and tied it on. It fit like a napkin. I walked into her kitchen, five foot ten, and I roared.

**[7. Desenlace]** (52 palabras)

She stared at me for a long time. Then she laughed so hard she had to sit down. "Dino," she said. "You got tall." And under the floor, I heard it. Footsteps on the basement stairs. One. Two. All fourteen. The basement door swung open. Nobody there. The bottom step was empty.

**[8. Remate]** (39 palabras)

Her basement is still full. I check it every Sunday. I'm never in it. But my own basement has one new thing on the shelf. A tag that says TELL GRANDMA ABOUT THE CRUSTS. It can stay down there.

30	**[1. Gancho]** (12 palabras)
31	
32	In this world, every EXCUSE you say out loud comes TRUE. Instantly.
33	
34	**[2. Ejemplos del mundo]** (54 palabras)
35	
36	Barnaby said his dog ate his homework. So his dog ate his homework. Then his backpack. Then one shoe. My mom said her phone died. We held a small funeral. Our bus driver blamed traffic. Now a raccoon directs traffic on Maple Street. And there are no TAKE-BACKS. Whatever you make up, you keep.
37	
38	**[3. El ángulo del narrador]** (34 palabras)
39	
40	I once told my cousin, "Sorry, can't. I have a thing." Poof. Now I have a THING. It's purple. It weighs nine pounds. It hums. It follows me everywhere, and it never has plans.
41	
42	**[4. Crisis]** (36 palabras)
43	
44	Then Delia invited me to her pool party. Saturday. She's been my best friend since kindergarten, and this was invite number seven. I dodged the first six. Because I'm fourteen and I can't SWIM. Nobody knows.
45	
46	**[5. Tres intentos fallidos]** (92 palabras)
47	
48	So I made excuses. Monday I said, "Can't. I'm helping my uncle move." I don't have an uncle. Poof. Uncle Rondo. Forty-three boxes, one piano, fifth floor, no elevator. We finished Thursday. He cried. I'd known him four days. Then I said, "I think I'm allergic to pools." Poof. I sneezed at a puddle. I sneezed at a glass of water. I sneezed at a picture of a lake. Friday I panicked. "We'll be out of town." Poof. Our whole HOUSE was out of town. In a field. Next to a cow.
49	
50	**[6. Cuarto intento]** (54 palabras)
51	
52	Saturday I walked six miles back, sneezing, carrying a nine-pound Thing. I stood at Delia's gate with no excuses left. "I can't swim," I said. "I never learned. I'm fourteen, and I'm scared of the shallow end. That's why I said no six times." I waited for the poof. Nothing. The truth doesn't POOF.
53	
54	**[7. Desenlace]** (75 palabras)
55	
56	Delia didn't laugh. She looked at her pool. Then she yelled, "Sorry, everybody! Our deep end is BROKEN!" Poof. The whole pool was TWO FEET deep. Everybody stood up, very confused. No take-backs. She did that to her own pool. Then the Thing waddled past us and hopped in. It floats. Of course it floats. I held on with both arms. And guess who was a lifeguard for twenty-two years? Uncle Rondo. He cried again.
57	
58	**[8. Remate]** (46 palabras)
59	
60	I can swim now. I sneeze the whole time, but I can swim. Delia's pool is still two feet deep. She says she'd do it again. She invited the Thing to her next party. It hummed, "Sorry, I have a thing." Poof. Now there are TWO.

174	**[1. Gancho]** (19 palabras)
175	
176	In this world, every pet writes a REVIEW of its owner, and it gets posted on your front door.
177	
178	**[2. Ejemplos del mundo]** (66 palabras)
179	
180	Every Saturday. Stars and everything. The dog next door gives five stars every week. "He dropped a meatball in 2021. I think about it daily." My cousin's goldfish wrote, "Three stars. Who is this guy." My aunt's parrot just posted her phone password. But five stars has a price. Mrs. Garza got five stars once. Now she has twenty-three cats, a goat, and a waiting list.
181	
182	**[3. El ángulo del narrador]** (47 palabras)
183	
184	My cat is named Dennis. Dennis has given me one star eight Saturdays in a row. "ONE STAR. He sings in the shower." "One star. Touched my belly in 2022. I remember." "One star. Gets home at 3:42. I wait at the window from 3:30. For nothing."
185	
186	**[4. Crisis]** (28 palabras)
187	
188	Here's the problem. Twelve one-star reviews in a row, and you LOSE your pet. The Pet Office moves it to a better home. I had four Saturdays left.
189	
190	**[5. Tres intentos fallidos]** (86 palabras)
191	
192	So I tried to buy a star. Week nine, I got the fancy salmon in the tiny gold can. Fourteen dollars. "One star. Salmon was fine. Service was slow." Week ten, I built a six-foot cat tower with four floors. "One star. I slept in the box. The box is drafty." Week eleven, I gave him my whole bed. I slept on the floor for seven nights. "HALF a star. He snores down there too." I didn't know half a star existed. Dennis found a way.
193	
194	**[6. Cuarto intento]** (61 palabras)
195	
196	Friday night, I quit. No salmon. No tower. I sat on the floor next to his box. "Okay. You WIN. If you want a better home, I'll carry your box there myself. But you're the first thing I look for when I open the door. Every single day." Then I cried on him a little. He allowed it for four seconds.
197	
198	**[7. Desenlace]** (58 palabras)
199	
200	Saturday morning, the review was on the door. I read it with one eye closed. "TWO stars. He cried on me. Disgusting. I'm STAYING. To every pet reading this door: he is TAKEN. Why do you think I kept him at one star?" I looked across the street. Twenty-three cats and a goat were staring at my door.
201

203	
204	Sunday, the goat was on my porch. Dennis handled it. Then he posted a second review. About the goat. ZERO stars.

305	
306	**[1. Gancho]** (18 palabras)
307	
308	In this town, you can only lie on TUESDAYS. The other six days, only the TRUTH comes out.
309	
310	**[2. Ejemplos del mundo]** (71 palabras)
311	
312	On Monday my teacher said we're her least favorite class. On Sunday Grandma said my sweater makes me look like a couch. So everybody saves the fake stuff for Tuesday. Birthday presents get opened on Tuesdays, so you can say "I love it." Dentists only work Tuesdays. "This won't hurt a bit." The weatherman says it's raining tacos. But there's a catch. NOBODY believes one word you say on a Tuesday.
313	
314	**[3. El ángulo del narrador]** (54 palabras)
315	
316	I keep a Tuesday List. Fourteen lies, ready to go. "I flossed." "Great meatloaf, Dad." And number fourteen. Tell Tess I like her. If she laughs, say "GOTCHA, it's Tuesday." I've done it thirty-one Tuesdays in a row. She laughs every time. Then every Wednesday she falls asleep in first period. Nobody knows why.
317	
318	**[4. Crisis]** (27 palabras)
319	
320	Last Monday, Tess told me her family is moving. Wednesday. Seven a.m. So I had one day left to say it. And that day was a Tuesday.
321	
322	**[5. Tres intentos fallidos]** (69 palabras)
323	
324	I tried to make a Tuesday count. First I just said it. "I like you. For REAL." She said, "Good one," and punched my arm. Then I wrote it on a card. She put it in a shoebox with nine other Tuesday cards. Then I went big. A forty-foot banner on the gym roof. TESS, I MEAN IT. Plus the whole drum line. She clapped. "Best Tuesday bit ever."
325	
326	**[6. Cuarto intento]** (71 palabras)
327	
328	That night I stared at my list. And I got it. Six days a week, she would have had to believe me. I picked the one day I could take it back. Thirty-one times. So at 11:58, I stood under her window. No banner. No drums. I waited two minutes. Longest two minutes of my life. At 12:01, on a WEDNESDAY, I said, "I like you. And I can't say gotcha."
329	
330	**[7. Desenlace]** (47 palabras)
331	
332	Her window was already open. She was already there. "FINALLY," she said. "I've stayed up past midnight thirty-one Tuesdays in a row. Just to see if you'd say it again on Wednesday." It was Wednesday. She couldn't be lying. So that's why she slept through first period.
333	
334	**[8. Remate]** (27 palabras)
335	
336	She still moved at seven a.m. It's forty minutes away. I visit every Wednesday. I threw out the Tuesday List. Okay, I kept one. Great meatloaf, Dad.

411	#### FILE 025-the-tunda.md
412	# Guion 025: The Tunda
413	
414	Guion original inspirado en la leyenda oral de **la Tunda**, del Pacífico
415	colombiano y de Esmeraldas (Ecuador), tradición de comunidades
416	afrodescendientes (`docs/05-guiones-y-fuentes.md`, sección de folclor
417	colombiano). Conteo real con script: **478 palabras** (rango pedido: 400 a
418	480). A 240 palabras por minuto son cerca de 120 segundos.
419	
420	- **Tema**: terror suave, familia (dos hermanos y una mamá que trabaja lejos)
421	- **Final**: emotivo (la mamá vuelve) con remate tierno y cómico
422	- **Regla**: en este pueblo, cuando tu mamá te llama desde los árboles, le
423	  miras los pies antes de contestar. Lo que vive en el manglar puede copiar
424	  la cara y la voz de quien amas, pero un pie siempre le sale de madera
425	- **Costo de la regla**: nadie puede mirar por ti; solo sirve si miras tú
426	  mismo. Si la sigues, te da camarones de río hasta que olvidas tu casa
427	- **Detalle sembrado**: "hago las tareas en las gradas de atrás, mirando
428	  hacia los árboles, todas las tardes hasta que oscurece" y "mi mamá silba
429	  pésimo, como una tetera que se rinde" (bloque 3). Se cosechan en los
430	  bloques 4, 6 y 8
431	- **Giro**: el narrador, el hermano responsable que conoce la regla, ya le
432	  había visto el pie de madera tres semanas atrás y aun así salía cada
433	  tarde solo para oírla decir su nombre. Extrañaba tanto a su mamá que una
434	  falsa le servía
435	- **Conteo real**: 478 palabras (19, 95, 67, 42, 93, 61, 65, 36), contadas con script
436	- **Título alterno**: In This Town, You Check Your Mother's Feet First
437	
438	## Narración
439	
440	El texto de la narración va en inglés, a ras de margen, listo para pegar en el
441	generador de voz. También está en `025-the-tunda.txt`.
442	
443	**[1. Gancho]** (19 palabras)
444	
445	In this town, when your mother calls you from the trees, you look at her FEET before you answer.
446	
447	**[2. Ejemplos del mundo]** (95 palabras)
448	
449	Something lives in the mangroves behind our houses. The old people call it the TUNDA. It can wear the face of anybody you love. It can do their voice. But it can never get one foot right. One foot is always WOOD. Carved like the stick Grandma uses to whip hot chocolate. So we check FEET. At the door. At dinner. My uncle checks his own every morning. Follow it, and it feeds you river shrimp until you forget your own house. One catch. Nobody can look for you. You have to look DOWN yourself.
450	
451	**[3. El ángulo del narrador]** (67 palabras)
452	
453	My mom went to the city for work eight months ago. She calls on Sundays. I always say we're fine. She used to whistle us in for dinner. Worst whistle alive. Like a kettle giving up. I'm fourteen. I cook the rice. I walk my little brother Ciro to school. And lately I do my homework on the back steps, facing the trees. Every evening, until dark.
454	
455	**[4. Crisis]** (42 palabras)
456	
457	Last Thursday at sunset, Ciro dropped his spoon. "Mom's home," he said. And he ran out the back door, into the mangroves. He's six. He didn't look down. From the trees, her voice called his name. Then a whistle. A PERFECT one.
458	
459	**[5. Tres intentos fallidos]** (93 palabras)
460	
461	I ran after him with the rice pot still in my hand. I found them by the black water. He was holding her hand. She had Mom's braid. Mom's yellow dress. I called his name ten times. He didn't turn around. I beat that pot like a drum. A hundred times. That's what the old people do when somebody gets taken. She smiled with my mom's mouth. So I grabbed his arm and pulled. He pulled back harder. "Go home," he said. "Mom's here." And she held out her other hand to me.
462	
463	**[6. Cuarto intento]** (61 palabras)
464	
465	I ALMOST took it. That's the part I never told anybody. "Ciro," I said. "I saw her three weeks ago. I looked at her feet the first night. I KNEW. I still sat on those steps every evening. Just to hear her say my name." My voice was shaking. "I didn't want to look either. But Mom can't WHISTLE. Look down."
466	
467	**[7. Desenlace]** (65 palabras)
468	
469	He looked. One bare foot. One foot of dark carved wood. He let go. She didn't chase us. Mom's face just went still, like a puddle when the wind stops. Then she walked back into the trees. Step, knock. Step, knock. I carried Ciro home. On Sunday the phone rang. For the first time, I didn't say we were fine. I said, "Mom. Come HOME."
470	
471	**[8. Remate]** (36 palabras)
472	
473	She got off the bus Tuesday. Ciro and I both looked down. Two muddy sandals. Then she tried to whistle. Kettle. Giving up. Best sound I ever heard. I still checked her feet twice at dinner.

# Guion 022: In This World, Excuses Become True

Guion original. Sale de la premisa 35 del banco (`docs/05-guiones-y-fuentes.md`,
sección de comedia). Conteo real con script: **403 palabras** (rango pedido
para comedia: 330 a 400). A 240 palabras por minuto son cerca de 101 segundos.

- **Tema**: comedia, amistad
- **Final**: cómico, con confesión sincera y un gesto de amistad antes del
  remate
- **Regla**: toda excusa dicha en voz alta se vuelve verdad al instante
- **Costo de la regla**: no hay devoluciones; te quedas para siempre con lo
  que inventaste
- **Detalle sembrado**: la Cosa ("I have a thing": morada, nueve libras,
  zumba, lo sigue a todas partes), bloque 3. Se cosecha en el bloque 7 (flota
  y le sirve de flotador) y en el remate. También el tío Rondo, inventado en
  el bloque 5, que resulta salvavidas
- **Giro**: cuando el narrador por fin dice la verdad, Delia no se ríe: grita
  una excusa a propósito ("Our deep end is broken!") y deja su propia piscina
  de dos pies de hondo para siempre. La regla, que todo el guion fue un
  castigo, se usa una vez como regalo, y con el mismo costo: sin devoluciones
- **Conteo real**: 403 palabras (12, 54, 34, 36, 92, 54, 75, 46), contadas con script
- **Título alterno**: No Take-Backs

## Narración

El texto de la narración va en inglés, a ras de margen, listo para pegar en el
generador de voz. También está en `022-excuses-become-true.txt`.

**[1. Gancho]** (12 palabras)

In this world, every EXCUSE you say out loud comes TRUE. Instantly.

**[2. Ejemplos del mundo]** (54 palabras)

Barnaby said his dog ate his homework. So his dog ate his homework. Then his backpack. Then one shoe. My mom said her phone died. We held a small funeral. Our bus driver blamed traffic. Now a raccoon directs traffic on Maple Street. And there are no TAKE-BACKS. Whatever you make up, you keep.

**[3. El ángulo del narrador]** (34 palabras)

I once told my cousin, "Sorry, can't. I have a thing." Poof. Now I have a THING. It's purple. It weighs nine pounds. It hums. It follows me everywhere, and it never has plans.

**[4. Crisis]** (36 palabras)

Then Delia invited me to her pool party. Saturday. She's been my best friend since kindergarten, and this was invite number seven. I dodged the first six. Because I'm fourteen and I can't SWIM. Nobody knows.

**[5. Tres intentos fallidos]** (92 palabras)

So I made excuses. Monday I said, "Can't. I'm helping my uncle move." I don't have an uncle. Poof. Uncle Rondo. Forty-three boxes, one piano, fifth floor, no elevator. We finished Thursday. He cried. I'd known him four days. Then I said, "I think I'm allergic to pools." Poof. I sneezed at a puddle. I sneezed at a glass of water. I sneezed at a picture of a lake. Friday I panicked. "We'll be out of town." Poof. Our whole HOUSE was out of town. In a field. Next to a cow.

**[6. Cuarto intento]** (54 palabras)

Saturday I walked six miles back, sneezing, carrying a nine-pound Thing. I stood at Delia's gate with no excuses left. "I can't swim," I said. "I never learned. I'm fourteen, and I'm scared of the shallow end. That's why I said no six times." I waited for the poof. Nothing. The truth doesn't POOF.

**[7. Desenlace]** (75 palabras)

Delia didn't laugh. She looked at her pool. Then she yelled, "Sorry, everybody! Our deep end is BROKEN!" Poof. The whole pool was TWO FEET deep. Everybody stood up, very confused. No take-backs. She did that to her own pool. Then the Thing waddled past us and hopped in. It floats. Of course it floats. I held on with both arms. And guess who was a lifeguard for twenty-two years? Uncle Rondo. He cried again.

**[8. Remate]** (46 palabras)

I can swim now. I sneeze the whole time, but I can swim. Delia's pool is still two feet deep. She says she'd do it again. She invited the Thing to her next party. It hummed, "Sorry, I have a thing." Poof. Now there are TWO.

**[1. Gancho]** (19 palabras)

**[2. Ejemplos del mundo]** (66 palabras)

Every Saturday. Stars and everything. The dog next door gives five stars every week. "He dropped a meatball in 2021. I think about it daily." My cousin's goldfish wrote, "Three stars. Who is this guy." My aunt's parrot just posted her phone password. But five stars has a price. Mrs. Garza got five stars once. Now she has twenty-three cats, a goat, and a waiting list.

**[3. El ángulo del narrador]** (47 palabras)

My cat is named Dennis. Dennis has given me one star eight Saturdays in a row. "ONE STAR. He sings in the shower." "One star. Touched my belly in 2022. I remember." "One star. Gets home at 3:42. I wait at the window from 3:30. For nothing."

**[4. Crisis]** (28 palabras)

Here's the problem. Twelve one-star reviews in a row, and you LOSE your pet. The Pet Office moves it to a better home. I had four Saturdays left.

So I tried to buy a star. Week nine, I got the fancy salmon in the tiny gold can. Fourteen dollars. "One star. Salmon was fine. Service was slow." Week ten, I built a six-foot cat tower with four floors. "One star. I slept in the box. The box is drafty." Week eleven, I gave him my whole bed. I slept on the floor for seven nights. "HALF a star. Friday night, I quit. No salmon. No tower. I sat on the floor next to his box. "Okay. You WIN. If you want a better home, I'll carry your box there myself. But you're the first thing I look for when I open the door. Every single day." Then I cried on him a little. He allowed it for four seconds.

#### FILE 024-you-can-only-lie-on-tuesdays.md
# Guion 024: In This Town, You Can Only Lie on Tuesdays

Guion original. Sale de la premisa 40 del banco (`docs/05-guiones-y-fuentes.md`,
sección de comedia). Conteo real con script: **384 palabras** (rango pedido
para comedia: 330 a 400). A 240 palabras por minuto son cerca de 96 segundos.

- **Tema**: comedia, primer amor (a nivel de "me gustas")
- **Final**: agridulce con remate cómico (ella se muda de todos modos)
- **Regla**: solo se puede mentir los martes; los otros seis días, si
  hablas, sale la verdad
- **Costo de la regla**: nadie cree ni una palabra de lo que se dice un
  martes
- **Detalle sembrado**: la Lista de los Martes con "Great meatloaf, Dad" y
  el punto catorce; y "todos los miércoles ella se duerme en la primera
  hora, nadie sabe por qué" (bloque 3). Se cosechan en los bloques 6, 7 y 8
- **Giro**: el problema nunca fue el martes. Tenía seis días a la semana en
  los que ella habría tenido que creerle, y escogió 31 veces el único día en
  que podía retractarse. Y ella llevaba 31 martes despierta hasta la
  medianoche, esperando que lo repitiera en miércoles
- **Conteo real**: 384 palabras (18, 71, 54, 27, 69, 71, 47, 27), contadas con script
- **Título alterno**: The Tuesday List

## Narración

El texto de la narración va en inglés, a ras de margen, listo para pegar en el
generador de voz. También está en `024-you-can-only-lie-on-tuesdays.txt`.

**[1. Gancho]** (18 palabras)

In this town, you can only lie on TUESDAYS. The other six days, only the TRUTH comes out.

**[2. Ejemplos del mundo]** (71 palabras)

On Monday my teacher said we're her least favorite class. On Sunday Grandma said my sweater makes me look like a couch. So everybody saves the fake stuff for Tuesday. Birthday presents get opened on Tuesdays, so you can say "I love it." Dentists only work Tuesdays. "This won't hurt a bit." The weatherman says it's raining tacos. But there's a catch. NOBODY believes one word you say on a Tuesday.

**[3. El ángulo del narrador]** (54 palabras)

I keep a Tuesday List. Fourteen lies, ready to go. "I flossed." "Great meatloaf, Dad." And number fourteen. Tell Tess I like her. If she laughs, say "GOTCHA, it's Tuesday." I've done it thirty-one Tuesdays in a row. She laughs every time. Then every Wednesday she falls asleep in first period. Nobody knows why.

**[4. Crisis]** (27 palabras)

Last Monday, Tess told me her family is moving. Wednesday. Seven a.m. So I had one day left to say it. And that day was a Tuesday.

**[5. Tres intentos fallidos]** (69 palabras)

I tried to make a Tuesday count. First I just said it. "I like you. For REAL." She said, "Good one," and punched my arm. Then I wrote it on a card. She put it in a shoebox with nine other Tuesday cards. Then I went big. A forty-foot banner on the gym roof. TESS, I MEAN IT. Plus the whole drum line. She clapped. "Best Tuesday bit ever."

**[6. Cuarto intento]** (71 palabras)

That night I stared at my list. And I got it. Six days a week, she would have had to believe me. I picked the one day I could take it back. Thirty-one times. So at 11:58, I stood under her window. # Guion 025: The Tunda

Guion original inspirado en la leyenda oral de **la Tunda**, del Pacífico
colombiano y de Esmeraldas (Ecuador), tradición de comunidades
afrodescendientes (`docs/05-guiones-y-fuentes.md`, sección de folclor
colombiano). Conteo real con script: **478 palabras** (rango pedido: 400 a
480). A 240 palabras por minuto son cerca de 120 segundos.

- **Tema**: terror suave, familia (dos hermanos y una mamá que trabaja lejos)
- **Final**: emotivo (la mamá vuelve) con remate tierno y cómico
- **Regla**: en este pueblo, cuando tu mamá te llama desde los árboles, le
  miras los pies antes de contestar. Lo que vive en el manglar puede copiar
  la cara y la voz de quien amas, pero un pie siempre le sale de madera
- **Costo de la regla**: nadie puede mirar por ti; solo sirve si miras tú
  mismo. Si la sigues, te da camarones de río hasta que olvidas tu casa
- **Detalle sembrado**: "hago las tareas en las gradas de atrás, mirando
  hacia los árboles, todas las tardes hasta que oscurece" y "mi mamá silba
  pésimo, como una tetera que se rinde" (bloque 3). Se cosechan en los
  bloques 4, 6 y 8
- **Giro**: el narrador, el hermano responsable que conoce la regla, ya le
  había visto el pie de madera tres semanas atrás y aun así salía cada
  tarde solo para oírla decir su nombre. Extrañaba tanto a su mamá que una
  falsa le servía
- **Conteo real**: 478 palabras (19, 95, 67, 42, 93, 61, 65, 36), contadas con script
- **Título alterno**: In This Town, You Check Your Mother's Feet First

## Narración

El texto de la narración va en inglés, a ras de margen, listo para pegar en el
generador de voz. También está en `025-the-tunda.txt`.

**[1. Gancho]** (19 palabras)

In this town, when your mother calls you from the trees, you look at her FEET before you answer.

**[2. Ejemplos del mundo]** (95 palabras)

Something lives in the mangroves behind our houses. The old people call it the TUNDA. It can wear the face of anybody you love. It can do their voice. But it can never get one foot right. One foot is always WOOD. Carved like the stick Grandma uses to whip hot chocolate. So we check FEET. At the door. At dinner. My uncle checks his own every morning. Follow it, and it feeds you river shrimp until you forget your own house. One catch. Nobody can look for you. You have to look DOWN yourself.

**[3. El ángulo del narrador]** (67 palabras)

My mom went to the city for work eight months ago. She calls on Sundays. I always say we're fine. She used to whistle us in for dinner. Worst whistle alive. Like a kettle giving up. I'm fourteen. I cook the rice. I walk my little brother Ciro to school. And lately I do my homework on the back steps, facing the trees. Every evening, until dark.

**[4. Crisis]** (42 palabras)

Last Thursday at sunset, Ciro dropped his spoon. "Mom's home," he said. And he ran out the back door, into the mangroves. He's six. He didn't look down. From the trees, her voice called his name. Then a whistle. A PERFECT one.

**[5. Tres intentos fallidos]** (93 palabras)

I ran after him with the rice pot still in my hand. I found them by the black water. He was holding her hand. She had Mom's braid. Mom's yellow dress. I called his name ten times. He didn't turn around. I beat that pot like a drum. A hundred times. That's what the old people do when somebody gets taken. She smiled with my mom's mouth. So I grabbed his arm and pulled. He pulled back harder. "Go home," he said. "Mom's here." And she held out her other hand to me.

**[6. Cuarto intento]** (61 palabras)

I ALMOST took it. That's the part I never told anybody. "Ciro," I said. "I saw her three weeks ago. I looked at her feet the first night. I KNEW. I still sat on those steps every evening. Just to hear her say my name." My voice was shaking. "I didn't want to look either. But Mom can't WHISTLE. Look down."

**[7. Desenlace]** (65 palabras)

He looked. One bare foot. One foot of dark carved wood. He let go. She didn't chase us. Mom's face just went still, like a puddle when the wind stops. Then she walked back into the trees. Step, knock. Step, knock. I carried Ciro home. On Sunday the phone rang. For the first time, I didn't say we were fine. I said, "Mom. Come HOME."

**[8. Remate]** (36 palabras)

She got off the bus Tuesday. Ciro and I both looked down. Two muddy sandals. Then she tried to whistle. Kettle. Giving up. Best sound I ever heard. I still checked her feet twice at dinner.

134	# Guion 015: In This School, Rumors Become Graffiti
135	
136	Guion original. Sale de la premisa 23 del banco
137	(`docs/05-guiones-y-fuentes.md`): cada chisme se escribe solo en las paredes y
138	solo se borra diciendo la verdad en voz alta.
139	
140	- **Tema**: colegio (un chisme inventado y la envidia de quien nadie nombra)
141	- **Final**: redención con ironía (el narrador recibe su primer chisme y decide
142	  no borrarlo)
143	- **Regla**: todo chisme se pinta solo en las paredes del colegio
144	- **Costo de la regla**: solo se borra cuando alguien dice la verdad completa
145	  en voz alta; ni jabón, ni carteles, ni medias verdades sirven
146	- **Detalle sembrado**: "nunca he salido en una pared, ni una letra" (bloque
147	  3). Se cosecha en el desenlace (aparece su primer grafiti) y en el remate (es
148	  el único chisme que nadie quiere borrar)
149	- **Giro**: el narrador inventó el chisme por envidia de ser invisible; al
150	  confesarlo, el niño al que le hizo daño le regala lo único que nunca tuvo:
151	  que alguien hable de él
152	- **Conteo real**: 357 palabras (20, 50, 31, 56, 75, 47, 58, 20), contadas con script
153	- **Título alterno**: The Gym Wall
154	
155	## Narración
156	
157	El texto de la narración va en inglés, a ras de margen, listo para pegar en el
158	generador de voz. También está en `015-rumors-become-graffiti.txt`.
159	
160	**[1. Gancho]**
161	
162	In this school, rumors paint themselves on the walls, and only come off when somebody says the truth out loud.
163	
164	**[2. Ejemplos del mundo]**
165	
166	The sixth-grade hall once said MR. PELLMAN WEARS A WIG, in green letters two feet tall. He walked up and said, "Yes. His name is Stanley." Gone in one second. The cafeteria wall says THE NUGGETS ARE MOSTLY CARROTS. The lunch lady refuses to comment. It's been up four years.
167	
168	**[3. El ángulo del narrador]**
169	
170	I've never been on a wall. Not one letter. Nine years in this school, and nobody has ever said a word about me. I told myself that was a good thing.
171	
172	**[4. Crisis]**
173	
174	Then Soren showed up. New kid. He could juggle oranges. By Friday, everybody knew his name. So at lunch I said, "I heard he got kicked out of his old school." I made it up. Monday morning, it was on the gym wall. Red letters, six feet tall. Soren stood under it, scrubbing with his sleeve.
175	
176	**[5. Tres intentos fallidos]**
177	
178	I tried to fix it quietly. Tuesday, I used two buckets of soap. The letters just got shinier. Wednesday, I taped a bake sale poster over it. The letters crawled onto the poster. BAKE SALE: SOREN GOT KICKED OUT. Thursday at six a.m., I stood alone in the gym and whispered, "It isn't true." One letter faded. Then it all came back, bigger, and spread across the ceiling. The wall doesn't take half a truth.
179	
180	**[6. Cuarto intento]**
181	
182	Friday, the gym was full. Pep rally. Four hundred kids. I took the microphone from the mascot. "I made it up," I said. My voice shook. "Soren's been here one week and everybody likes him. I've been here nine years, and nobody even knows my middle name."
183	
184	**[7. Desenlace]**
185	
186	The letters peeled off like old tape. The wall went white. Nobody clapped. Soren looked at me for a long time. Then he walked out. Monday, there was new writing over my locker. Small. Blue. HENRIK'S MIDDLE NAME IS PROBABLY SOMETHING COOL. LIKE WOLFGANG. Soren walked past, juggling one orange. He didn't look at me. He was smiling.
187	
188	**[8. Remate]**
189	
190	It's Eugene. I am never saying that out loud. It's the only rumor in this school nobody wants to erase.
191

259	# Guion 016: In This School, the Quietest Kid Controls the Weather
260	
261	Guion original. Sale de la premisa 25 del banco
262	(`docs/05-guiones-y-fuentes.md`): el clima del colegio depende del ánimo de
263	quien menos habla.
264	
265	- **Tema**: colegio (el niño callado y el niño que no se calla)
266	- **Final**: cálido y cómico, con intercambio de papeles
267	- **Regla**: el clima sobre el colegio sigue el ánimo del que menos habla
268	- **Costo de la regla**: el más callado no puede esconder lo que siente; cada
269	  vez que se mueve una nube, 600 niños voltean a mirarlo
270	- **Detalle sembrado**: "yo soy el que más habla, así que el cielo nunca ha
271	  sido mi problema" y el récord de 19 minutos sin respirar (bloque 3). Se
272	  cosechan en el bloque 6 (al callarse, el cielo pasa a ser suyo) y en el
273	  desenlace (Tobin habla 19 minutos)
274	- **Giro**: el narrador se calla un día entero para quitarle el cielo de
275	  encima a Tobin, y el colegio entero ve lo que siente por dentro el que más
276	  habla: niebla nerviosa
