280	## Narración
281	
282	El texto de la narración va en inglés, a ras de margen, listo para pegar en el
283	generador de voz. También está en `016-quietest-kid-controls-the-weather.txt`.
284	
285	**[1. Gancho]**
286	
287	In this school, the weather over the building follows the MOOD of the kid who talks the LEAST.
288	
289	**[2. Ejemplos del mundo]**
290	
291	That kid is Tobin. He said eleven words all last year. Nine of them were "here." When he aced a spelling test, we got sun for a week. When he dropped his sandwich, it hailed on the parking lot. Our weather app is just a photo of his face. And every time a cloud moves, six hundred kids turn around and stare at him.
292	
293	**[3. El ángulo del narrador]**
294	
295	Me, I talk the MOST. Teachers have timed it. My record is nineteen minutes without a breath. So the sky has never once been my problem.
296	
297	**[4. Crisis]**
298	
299	Then came Field Day week. It rained nine days straight. Principal Ruiz said if it rained Friday, Field Day became a three-hour assembly about fire exits. Everybody looked at Tobin. Then everybody looked at me. "I'll fix him," I said.
300	
301	**[5. Tres intentos fallidos]**
302	
303	First, cupcakes. Fourteen of them, stacked on his desk. We got four minutes of sun. Then fog. Second, the marching band played his favorite song under his window. Hail, the size of meatballs. The tuba filled up. Third, I got six hundred kids in the gym chanting WE LOVE TOBIN. Lightning hit the flagpole. Twice. Tobin ran.
304	
305	**[6. Cuarto intento]**
306	
307	I found him under a library table. I opened my mouth. And for the first time in my life, I CLOSED it. I sat down next to him. I said NOTHING. Not that afternoon. Not all of Thursday. The nurse took my temperature. Tobin said "here" at attendance. I didn't. By noon, the rain stopped. The sky was mine now.
308	
309	**[7. Desenlace]**
310	
311	It wasn't sunny. It was fog. Thick, nervous fog, with one tiny cloud going in circles. Six hundred kids turned around and stared at me. Now they knew what the loud kid looks like on the inside. Tobin looked up at my fog. Then he said three words. "Oh. You TOO?" And he started talking. About frogs. For nineteen minutes. Nobody was watching him. The fog burned off.
312	
313	**[8. Remate]**
314	
315	Friday, I kept my mouth shut. Seventy-four and sunny. Tobin won the sack race, screaming the whole way. We take turns now. I've got the sky on Mondays. Bring a jacket.

417	
418	**[1. Gancho]**
419	
420	In this world, your backpack weighs exactly as much as your WORRIES, and emptying it doesn't HELP.
421	
422	**[2. Ejemplos del mundo]**
423	
424	My math teacher wheels hers in on a cart. During finals week, the school bus drags sparks down the road. Babies' diaper bags float. Parents tie them to the stroller like balloons. My grandma's purse weighs nothing. She says she ran out at seventy.
425	
426	**[3. El ángulo del narrador]**
427	
428	Mine FLOATS too. I'm fifteen, and I tie my backpack to my wrist so it won't blow away. Dad calls me "the kite." My little brother Benji is the happiest kid in fourth grade. Gap-tooth grin. Sings to the toaster. And every morning, he drags his bag to the bus with both hands.
429	
430	**[4. Crisis]**
431	
432	The morning he left for Camp Wobbly Pine, his bag wouldn't MOVE at all. It had cracked his bedroom floor. The bus left at eight. It was 7:31. Benji kept grinning. "It's FINE! I'll just live here now."
433	
434	**[5. Tres intentos fallidos]**
435	
436	I told him my best joke. He laughed for a full minute. The bag lost four ounces. So I emptied it. Two socks, a toothbrush, a frog flashlight. Still stuck. So I tied it to Dad's riding mower and hit the gas. The mower did a wheelie. The bag didn't budge. 7:48.
437	
438	**[6. Cuarto intento]**
439	
440	So I sat on the floor next to it. "Benji. What's in there?" He stopped grinning. "You wouldn't get it. Yours FLOATS." I untied my bag from my wrist and unzipped it. "Then put ONE in mine." He looked at me for a while. "Mom's car makes a noise." My bag dropped an inch. "Okay. That one's MINE now."
441	
442	**[7. Desenlace]**
443	
444	He kept going. Dad's job. The stove. If I'd pass math. If I packed my lunch. If I'd forget him when I got my license. Six worries. Half of them were about me. My bag hit the floor so hard the frog flashlight turned on. Benji picked his up with one hand. Mine had been floating for years because he was carrying my HALF.
445	
446	**[8. Remate]**
447	
448	He made the bus by nine seconds. My backpack weighs nineteen pounds now. I checked the stove twice today. Dad stopped calling me the kite. BEST backache I've ever had.

29	generador de voz. También está en `018-the-echo.txt`.
30	
31	**[1. Gancho]**
32	
33	In this town, the echo doesn't repeat what you say. It says what you really think.
34	
35	**[2. Ejemplos del mundo]**
36	
37	It lives in the Notch, a crack in the hills past the last streetlight. It answers in your own voice, one breath late, and the whole town hears it. Mr. Dabney once yelled, "I love it here!" The Notch said, "I'd leave tomorrow." He moved in June. Our mayor gave one speech up there. That's why we have a new mayor. So we whisper. All of us. We clap at football games like it's golf. Even the dogs bark quietly.
38	
39	**[3. El ángulo del narrador]**
40	
41	Only one person ever got her own words back. My mom. Every night she leaned off the back porch and yelled, "Goodnight, bug!" And the hills said it right back, word for word. We lost her last winter. Now Dad says the same thing every morning. "We're doing great, kiddo." Thumbs up. Burnt toast.
42	
43	**[4. Crisis]**
44	
45	Then the night echoes started. 2:07 a.m. A man's voice rolled down off the hills, loud enough to rattle the spoons. "I can't do this." Nobody heard a shout. Just the answer. Every dog in town went under a bed.
46	
47	**[5. Tres intentos fallidos]**
48	
49	The second night, it came again. "The house is too quiet." Forty windows lit up at once. I got up and checked Dad's room. The bed was empty. His boots were gone. The third night, I followed his boot prints up the trail with a flashlight. The fog swallowed the beam three feet out. Somebody was shouting up ahead. I found him at the edge of the Notch, hands cupped around his mouth. "I'M FINE!" he yelled into the dark. One breath. Then the dark answered in his voice. "I don't know how to be both of them." He yelled it seven times. It never once agreed.
50	
51	**[6. Cuarto intento]**
52	
53	I stepped up beside him. He jumped. "Go home, kiddo. We're doing great." Thumbs up. His thumb was shaking. So I turned to the Notch and yelled the only thing I had. "I'M FINE TOO!" One breath. Then my own voice came back, small and clear. "I hear you leave every night. I'm scared you won't come back."
54	
55	**[7. Desenlace]**
56	
57	Dad's thumb came down. He didn't say anything. He just took my hand. Then we yelled together, as loud as we could. "WE MISS YOU!" One breath. And the hills did something they hadn't done in a year. They said it back. Word for word.
58	
59	**[8. Remate]**
60	
61	The night echoes stopped. Dad still burns the toast, but he quit the thumbs up. And last night, half asleep, I heard the hills one more time. Two words. "Goodnight, bug." Nobody had yelled it. Somebody was just thinking it.

173	
174	**[1. Gancho]**
175	
176	In this town, something takes ONE thing from your house every night, and leaves one thing you LOST years ago.
177	
178	**[2. Ejemplos del mundo]**
179	
180	It comes at three a.m. You never see it. You just hear a drawer slide open, slow. It took our TV remote and left a sock I lost in second grade. The sock was still wet. It took Dad's car keys and left his retainer from high school. The Fitzgeralds lost a couch and got back a hamster. The hamster looked like it had seen things. The trade is always FAIR. Small for small. Big for big. And you don't get to pick.
181	
182	**[3. El ángulo del narrador]**
183	
184	My Nana isn't scared of it. She calls it "our night guest" and leaves a cup of tea by the pantry. By morning, the tea is gone. The cup never is. Nana used to call me Pidge. Since March, she calls me "the NICE GIRL." She lost my name somewhere, and she can't find it.
185	
186	**[4. Crisis]**
187	
188	So I had an idea. If our night guest brings back lost things, it could bring back that. Dad says by summer, she might lose his name too. I just had to offer something big enough.
189	
190	**[5. Tres intentos fallidos]**
191	
192	Night one, I left my bike by the pantry. In the morning, there was a tricycle I lost when I was four. Still muddy. Nana patted my hand. "Thank you, nice girl." Night two, I left my phone. I got Nana's reading glasses, missing since 2015. She put them on and read me the cereal box. Twice. Night three, I left everything. My savings jar, two hundred and twelve dollars. My trophies. The TV. In the morning, the kitchen was full. Forty-one umbrellas. Nine library books. Every mitten our family ever dropped. Nana clapped. "What a lovely sale. Do you work here?"
193	
194	**[6. Cuarto intento]**
195	
196	Night four, I left NOTHING. I sat at the kitchen table in the dark and waited. 2:59. The fridge stopped humming. 3:00. The pantry door opened by itself, one inch. The air went cold. Something was breathing in there, slow, like a drawer sliding. I didn't look. "I don't have anything left," I whispered. "So take something of mine. Anything. I won't even ask what. Just give her back one morning." The breathing stopped. The tea went down, like somebody sipping. The door clicked shut.
197	
198	**[7. Desenlace]**
199	
200	In the morning, the table was empty. First time ever. Nana shuffled in, squinting at the floor. "PIDGE," she said. "Why is there a tricycle in my kitchen?" I couldn't talk. She made pancakes. She beat me at cards, cheating. By dinner, I was "the nice girl" again.
201	
202	**[8. Remate]**
203	
204	There's a clean square in the dust on my shelf. I don't know what used to sit there. Now I know how Nana feels. It still takes one thing every night. But last night, for the first time, it WASHED the cup.

317	**[1. Gancho]** (11 palabras)
318	
319	In this town, nobody opens the door after the THIRD knock.
320	
321	**[2. Ejemplos del mundo]** (82 palabras)
322	
323	Two knocks is a neighbor. THREE knocks is something else. Nobody knows what, because nobody has opened in sixty-one years. So everybody here knocks twice. The mailman. The pizza guy. A woodpecker got a ticket. The thing that knocks three times picks one house. Always the newest family in town. Then it comes back every night at 9:14. And nobody visits a house that's got it. The Pruitts had it for six years. They finally moved. It knocked on the moving truck.
324	
325	**[3. El ángulo del narrador]** (48 palabras)
326	
327	We moved here in June. My fifth town in six years. New families here always get a welcome pie. We got nothing. Because on our first night, at 9:14, there it was. Knock. Knock. Knock. The third one is always softer than the first two. Like it's SORRY.
328	
329	**[4. Crisis]** (49 palabras)
330	
331	Four months later, my little brother Otis sleeps in the bathtub. It's the farthest spot from the front door. Then Mom started taping up boxes. "We leave Friday," she said. I had just unpacked my last one. I was not going to be the new kid a sixth time.
332	
333	**[5. Tres intentos fallidos]** (76 palabras)
334	
335	So I tried to make it stop. Monday, I taped a sign on the door. NOBODY HOME. It knocked three times on the sign. Tuesday, I slept with two pillows over my head. It knocked on my window. My room is on the second floor. Wednesday, I yelled through the door. "Go away! Nobody wants you here!" Ten seconds of nothing. Then three knocks, so quiet I almost missed them. Somehow that was the worst one.
336	
337	**[6. Cuarto intento]** (60 palabras)
338	
339	Thursday night, I sat on the floor with my back against the door. 9:14. Knock. Knock. Knock. And I said, "I'm sorry I yelled. I've been the new kid five times. I know what it's like to stand outside and hope somebody opens." Nothing. So I did the one thing you never do in this town. I OPENED the door.
340	
341	**[7. Desenlace]** (86 palabras)
342	
343	It was nine feet tall. A long gray raincoat with nothing inside but fog. No face. And it was holding a pie. Its hands shook so hard the tin rattled. There was a card on top. WELCOME TO TOWN, in handwriting from sixty-one years ago. I asked, "Why three knocks?" It looked down at where its feet should be. Its voice sounded like an old hinge. "TWO is for neighbors." It didn't think it was one. I said, "You've lived here longer than anybody. Knock TWICE."
344	
345	**[8. Remate]** (39 palabras)
346	
347	We unpacked the boxes. Otis sleeps in a bed again. We did not eat the pie. That pie is older than my grandpa. But every night at 9:14, there are two knocks on our door. And somebody always opens.

455	In this world, everything you forget ends up in your basement.
456	
457	**[2. Ejemplos del mundo]** (74 palabras)
458	
459	Keys. Homework. The name of that one actor. You go downstairs and there it is, on a shelf with a paper tag. My dad's basement has four hundred passwords and one wedding anniversary. Mom knew exactly which shelf. Our dog forgot a tennis ball in 2019. He still visits it. But there's a catch. You can't carry somebody else's forgotten thing back upstairs. 462	
463	My grandma lives two streets over. She calls me Dino. When I was seven, I wore a green dinosaur cape for a whole year. I'm fifteen now, and she still cuts the crusts off my sandwiches. I've wanted to tell her to stop since sixth grade. Lately her basement has been filling up. Her glasses. Her lemon cake recipe. The word "umbrella."
464	
465	**[4. Crisis]** (71 palabras)
466	
467	Last Sunday she smiled at me like I was the mailman. "Can I help you, young man?" I laughed. She didn't. So I went down to her basement. Fourteen steps. It was colder than it should have been. 470	
471	So I tried to bring me back up. I showed her forty photos of us. She said, "What a handsome boy. His grandma must be proud." Then I taped my school ID to her fridge. By lunch it was on a basement shelf. Then I took the other me by the hand and pulled him upstairs. Step eleven. Step twelve. On step thirteen he went thin, like breath on a window. Then he was back at the bottom, facing the wall.

474	
475	I sat down at her kitchen table. She put a plate in front of me. A sandwich, crusts cut off. "My grandson likes them like this," she said. "He's about this tall." Her hand stopped at the edge of the counter. She hadn't forgotten me. She forgot I grew up. So I quit trying to make her remember fifteen. I dug the green cape out of her hall closet and tied it on. It fit like a napkin. I walked into her kitchen, five foot ten, and I roared.

412	# Guion 025: The Tunda
413	
414	Guion original inspirado en la leyenda oral de **la Tunda**, del Pacífico
415	colombiano y de Esmeraldas (Ecuador), tradición de comunidades
416	afrodescendientes (`docs/05-guiones-y-fuentes.md`, sección de folclor
417	colombiano). Conteo real con script: **478 palabras** (rango pedido: 400 a
418	480). A 240 palabras por minuto son cerca de 120 segundos.

421	- **Final**: emotivo (la mamá vuelve) con remate tierno y cómico
422	- **Regla**: en este pueblo, cuando tu mamá te llama desde los árboles, le
423	  miras los pies antes de contestar. Lo que vive en el manglar puede copiar
424	  la cara y la voz de quien amas, pero un pie siempre le sale de madera
425	- **Costo de la regla**: nadie puede mirar por ti; solo sirve si miras tú
426	  mismo. Si la sigues, te da camarones de río hasta que olvidas tu casa
427	- **Detalle sembrado**: "hago las tareas en las gradas de atrás, mirando
428	  hacia los árboles, todas las tardes hasta que oscurece" y "mi mamá silba
429	  pésimo, como una tetera que se rinde" (bloque 3). Se cosechan en los
430	  bloques 4, 6 y 8
431	- **Giro**: el narrador, el hermano responsable que conoce la regla, ya le
432	  había visto el pie de madera tres semanas atrás y aun así salía cada
433	  tarde solo para oírla decir su nombre. Extrañaba tanto a su mamá que una
434	  falsa le servía

441	generador de voz. También está en `025-the-tunda.txt`.
442	
443	**[1. Gancho]** (19 palabras)
444	
445	In this town, when your mother calls you from the trees, you look at her FEET before you answer.
446	
447	**[2. Ejemplos del mundo]** (95 palabras)
448	
449	Something lives in the mangroves behind our houses. The old people call it the TUNDA. It can wear the face of anybody you love. It can do their voice. But it can never get one foot right. One foot is always WOOD. Carved like the stick Grandma uses to whip hot chocolate. So we check FEET. At the door. At dinner. My uncle checks his own every morning. Follow it, and it feeds you river shrimp until you forget your own house. One catch. Nobody can look for you. You have to look DOWN yourself.
450	
451	**[3. El ángulo del narrador]** (67 palabras)
452	
453	My mom went to the city for work eight months ago. She calls on Sundays. I always say we're fine. She used to whistle us in for dinner. Worst whistle alive. Like a kettle giving up. I'm fourteen. I cook the rice. I walk my little brother Ciro to school. And lately I do my homework on the back steps, facing the trees. Every evening, until dark.
454	
455	**[4. Crisis]** (42 palabras)
456	
457	Last Thursday at sunset, Ciro dropped his spoon. "Mom's home," he said. And he ran out the back door, into the mangroves. He's six. He didn't look down. From the trees, her voice called his name. Then a whistle. A PERFECT one.
458

He pulled back harder. "Go home," he said. "Mom's here." And she held out her other hand to me.
462

memoria, demasiado cerca de este tema. Dentro de la narración la criatura
  ya no tiene nombre propio: la narradora usa el apodo de la abuela, "our
  night guest". Los archivos pasaron de `019-the-borrower` a
  `019-the-night-trade`. En el banco de premisas (`docs/05`, premisa 31) sigue
  figurando con el nombre viejo; esa carpeta no se tocó en esta revisión.
  Falta repetir la búsqueda en YouTube con el título nuevo antes de producir.
- **Borradores**: tres pasadas. En la primera la narradora veía a la criatura;
  se quitó porque el miedo funcionaba mejor con la rendija negra y la
  respiración. En la segunda la tercera noche devolvía el anillo de bodas de
  Nana; se cambió por la cocina llena de paraguas, que falla peor y da la
  frase "Do you work here?". En la tercera se decidió que la mañana dure solo
  hasta la cena: sin ese límite el final no era agridulce.
- **Título y mayúsculas (2026-11-13)**: el título pasó de "The Borrower" a "The Night Trade" y se
  agregó el título alterno "In This Town, Something Takes One Thing Every Night". Motivo: la medición de 360 Shorts de
  canales líderes (`docs/08`) muestra que en inglés los títulos no llevan
  palabras en mayúsculas sostenidas ni pasan de 10 palabras. Dentro de la
  narración sí se marcaron palabras clave en MAYÚSCULAS (en el `.md` y en el
  `.txt`) para resaltarlas en los subtítulos; el texto es el mismo.

  roblox story" y la regla escrita, "something takes one thing every night
  and leaves something roblox story"): no hay ningún video con la misma idea.

  indique esta premisa; no se abrió). Ninguno trata de algo que se lleva un
  objeto cada noche y devuelve uno perdido. Queda anotado el homónimo: es un
  título de libro, no de un video del formato, y los títulos no se protegen
  por derecho de autor, pero si prefieres evitarlo, el título alterno "In This
  Town, Something Takes One Thing Every Night" no tiene coincidencias. Límite
  de la búsqueda: solo los 8 primeros resultados de cada consulta y por
  título.
